records.source: שִׁמְע֞וּ אֶת־הַדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֨ר אָנֹכִ֜י נֹשֵׂ֧א עֲלֵיכֶ֛ם קִינָ֖ה בֵּ֥ית יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: Hear the word the this which I [am] lifting up over you, a lament, house of Israel.
pieces: Hear this word, house of Israel, this lament I raise over you:

L.1: Hear this word, which I am taking up over you as a lament, house of Israel:

R.1: People of Israel, listen to this funeral song I am singing about you:

decisions.choice: a lament: a funeral song sung over the dead
decisions.reason: The word qinah is used for the song that mourners sang over someone who had died, as David did over Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:17). Amos sings it over Israel while the nation is still alive and prosperous, as if it were already dead. The short poem that follows (verse 2) has the uneven rhythm of such songs, a longer line followed by a shorter one, as in Lamentations.

decisions.choice: I: the prophet speaks, and the Lord GOD's words follow in verse 3
decisions.reason: The speaker takes up the lament himself, and in verse 3 he passes on what the Lord GOD says. As elsewhere in the book, the prophet's words and the LORD's run together without a break, and neither takes quotation marks.

decisions.choice: raise (B); funeral song ... singing (R); People of Israel (R)
decisions.reason: To 'lift up' a lament is to begin singing it aloud, so Balanced says 'raise'. Readable says 'funeral song', so that readers know what kind of song it is (m1), and 'people of Israel' for 'house of Israel', since 'house' here means the whole family of Israel's descendants.

records.heading: A lament for Israel

records.source: נָֽפְלָה֙ לֹֽא־תוֹסִ֣יף ק֔וּם בְּתוּלַ֖ת יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל נִטְּשָׁ֥ה עַל־אַדְמָתָ֖הּ אֵ֥ין מְקִימָֽהּ׃
records.gloss: She has fallen, she will not again rise, [the] virgin of Israel; she has been forsaken on her land, there [is] none raising her up.
pieces: Fallen, never to rise again, is Virgin Israel; \q she lies abandoned on her own land, with no one to lift her up.

L.2: Fallen, she will not rise again, the virgin Israel; \q forsaken on her land, there [is] no one to raise her up.

R.2: Israel, like a young woman, has fallen, \q and she will never get up again. \q She lies deserted on her own land, with no one to help her up.

decisions.choice: the virgin Israel: the nation pictured as a young woman not yet married
decisions.reason: The phrase pictures the whole people as a young woman. In a funeral song it adds to the grief: she has died young, before her life was full. Jeremiah uses the same picture (Jeremiah 31:4, 21).

decisions.choice: she has fallen ... she has been forsaken: spoken as already done
decisions.reason: The verbs are past tense. Israel was still standing and prosperous when Amos spoke, but the lament speaks of its fall as already certain, as if the funeral had begun.

decisions.choice: Virgin Israel (B, as Jeremiah 31:4); Israel, like a young woman (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced writes 'Virgin Israel' as a name, as Jeremiah 31:4 does. Readable keeps the picture of a young woman but makes Israel the subject, since 'virgin' as a title for a nation is unfamiliar.

records.source: כִּ֣י כֹ֤ה אָמַר֙ אֲדֹנָ֣י יְהוִ֔ה הָעִ֛יר הַיֹּצֵ֥את אֶ֖לֶף תַּשְׁאִ֣יר מֵאָ֑ה וְהַיּוֹצֵ֥את מֵאָ֛ה תַּשְׁאִ֥יר עֲשָׂרָ֖ה לְבֵ֥ית יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃ס
records.gloss: For thus says [the] Lord Yahweh: the city that goes out a thousand will have left a hundred, and that goes out a hundred will have left ten, for [the] house of Israel.
pieces: For the Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} says this: \q The city that marches out a thousand strong will be left with a hundred, \q and the one that marches out a hundred strong will be left with ten, in the house of Israel.

L.3: For thus says the Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}}: \q The city that goes out a thousand [strong] will have a hundred left, \q and [the one] that goes out a hundred [strong] will have ten left, to the house of Israel.

R.3: This is what the Lord {{divine_name:GOD|Yahweh}} says: \q When a city of Israel sends out a thousand soldiers, only a hundred will survive. \q When a town sends out a hundred, only ten will be left.

decisions.choice: goes out a thousand: sends out a thousand men to war
decisions.reason: A city 'went out' when its fighting men marched out to battle, and a town's troops were counted in units of a thousand and a hundred (1 Samuel 8:12; 2 Samuel 18:1). Nine out of ten will be lost. The remnant left is too small to be a comfort.

decisions.choice: to the house of Israel: this is what Israel will have left
alternatives: a note on the whole saying: 'so it will be for the house of Israel'
decisions.reason: The phrase stands at the end of the verse and says whose army this is. It may belong to the last clause ('ten left to the house of Israel') or to the whole saying ('so it will be for the house of Israel'). The sense is the same.

decisions.choice: Thus says the Lord GOD (L); The Lord GOD says this (B); This is what the Lord GOD says (R)
decisions.reason: The formula koh 'amar keeps the wording settled for Isaiah and Jeremiah at each level, with 'the Lord GOD' for Adonai with the divine name.

decisions.choice: of Israel; soldiers; survive (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says 'soldiers' and 'survive' to make plain that the city's fighting men are meant and that only a tenth of them will live (m1). It moves 'Israel' into the first sentence, where the reader needs it.

records.source: כִּ֣י כֹ֥ה אָמַ֛ר יְהוָ֖ה לְבֵ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל דִּרְשׁ֖וּנִי וִֽחְיֽוּ׃
records.gloss: For thus says Yahweh to [the] house of Israel: seek me and live.
pieces: For {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says this to the house of Israel: \q Seek {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and live!

L.4: For thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} to the house of Israel: \q Seek {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} and live!

R.4: This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says to the people of Israel: \q Seek {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, and you will live.

decisions.choice: seek me: turn to the LORD himself, to worship and obey him
decisions.reason: To 'seek' the LORD was to go to him in worship and prayer, to ask his will and follow it. Verse 5 sets this against going to the shrines: seeking the LORD is not the same as visiting his holy places. Verses 14-15 say what it means in practice: seek good, hate evil, and set up justice in the courts.

decisions.choice: and live: a promise as well as a command
decisions.reason: Two commands joined by 'and' in Hebrew often mean 'do this, and then this will follow'. Life here is the nation's survival, set against the funeral song of verses 1-2.

records.heading: Seek {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and live

records.source: וְאַֽל־תִּדְרְשׁוּ֙ בֵּֽית־אֵ֔ל וְהַגִּלְגָּל֙ לֹ֣א תָבֹ֔אוּ וּבְאֵ֥ר שֶׁ֖בַע לֹ֣א תַעֲבֹ֑רוּ כִּ֤י הַגִּלְגָּל֙ גָּלֹ֣ה יִגְלֶ֔ה וּבֵֽית־אֵ֖ל יִהְיֶ֥ה לְאָֽוֶן׃
records.gloss: And do not seek Bethel, and [to] Gilgal do not go, and [to] Beersheba do not cross over; for Gilgal will surely go into exile, and Bethel will become nothing.
pieces: Do not seek Bethel; \q do not go to Gilgal \q or cross over to Beersheba. \q For Gilgal is sure to go into exile, \q and Bethel will be reduced to nothing.

L.5: But do not seek Bethel, \q and do not go to Gilgal, \q and do not cross over to Beersheba; \q for Gilgal will certainly go into exile, \q and Bethel will become nothing.

R.5: Do not go to Bethel to worship. \q Do not go to Gilgal, \q or cross the border to Beersheba. \q The people of Gilgal will be taken away as captives, \q and Bethel will become nothing.

decisions.choice: Bethel, Gilgal, Beersheba: the great shrines where Israel worshiped
decisions.reason: Bethel was the royal shrine of the northern kingdom (7:13; 1 Kings 12:29-33), and Gilgal was another famous holy place (4:4; Hosea 4:15). Beersheba lay far to the south in Judah, so people from the north had to 'cross over' the border to go there on pilgrimage (8:14). All three were linked with the stories of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, or with Israel's entry into the land.

decisions.choice: a play on the names: Gilgal will go into exile, and Bethel ('house of God') will become nothing
decisions.reason: In Hebrew, 'Gilgal will surely go into exile' repeats the sounds of the name: haggilgal galoh yigleh. Bethel means 'house of God', and Amos says it will become 'aven, 'nothing' or 'trouble'. Hosea plays on the same word when he calls the town Beth-aven, 'house of nothing' (Hosea 4:15). The puns cannot be carried into translation, so a note gives them.

decisions.choice: go to Bethel to worship; cross the border; the people of Gilgal ... as captives (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says why people went to these towns, and that going to Beersheba meant crossing into Judah (m1). It says that the people of Gilgal will be taken away, since a town 'goes into exile' when its people are deported.

records.source: דִּרְשׁ֥וּ אֶת־יְהוָ֖ה וִֽחְי֑וּ פֶּן־יִצְלַ֤ח כָּאֵשׁ֙ בֵּ֣ית יוֹסֵ֔ף וְאָכְלָ֥ה וְאֵין־מְכַבֶּ֖ה לְבֵֽית־אֵֽל׃
records.gloss: Seek Yahweh and live, lest he rush like fire [on] the house of Joseph, and it devour, and there [is] none quenching [it] for Bethel.
pieces: Seek {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and live, \q or {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will sweep through the house of Joseph like fire; \q it will burn, and there will be no one at Bethel to put it out.

L.6: Seek {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and live, \q lest {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} break out like fire [against] the house of Joseph, \q and it devour, with no one to quench [it] for Bethel.

R.6: Seek {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, and you will live. \q If you do not, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will rush on Israel like a fire. \q It will burn everything, and no one at Bethel will be able to put it out.

decisions.choice: the house of Joseph: the northern kingdom
decisions.reason: Joseph was the father of Ephraim and Manasseh, the largest tribes of the north, so 'the house of Joseph' stands for the northern kingdom of Israel (also 5:15; 6:6).

decisions.choice: for Bethel: the fire will reach Bethel, and the shrine can do nothing to stop it
decisions.reason: The fire will burn at Bethel and no one there will put it out. The shrine the people trusted cannot protect them; the fire may even begin there (compare 3:14).

decisions.choice: If you do not; Israel (R)
decisions.reason: Readable spells out 'lest' as 'If you do not', and says 'Israel' for 'the house of Joseph', since the name stands for the northern kingdom (m1).

records.source: הַהֹפְכִ֥ים לְלַעֲנָ֖ה מִשְׁפָּ֑ט וּצְדָקָ֖ה לָאָ֥רֶץ הִנִּֽיחוּ׃
records.gloss: [O you] who turn into wormwood justice, and righteousness to [the] earth they cast down.
pieces: You turn justice into bitter wormwood \q and throw righteousness to the ground.

L.7: [You] who turn justice into wormwood, \q and cast righteousness down to the earth!

R.7: You turn justice into something bitter. \q You throw what is right to the ground.

decisions.choice: those who turn: a new address, naming the people Amos accuses
alternatives: read as 'Woe to those who turn', as 5:18 and 6:1 begin
decisions.reason: The verse opens with 'the ones who turn', without a main verb, and then changes to 'they' in the second line. It reads like the start of a 'woe' saying such as 5:18 and 6:1, and it may be that the word 'woe' was once said or written before it. The Hebrew as it stands still names those who are accused, and the sense is the same either way.

decisions.choice: justice and righteousness: fair judgment in the courts and right dealing with others
decisions.reason: Mishpat is justice as it is done, above all in the courts at the city gate (verses 10, 12, 15). Tsedaqah is what is right: keeping faith with others, the poor above all. The pair runs through the book (5:24; 6:12). Here those Amos accuses turn justice into something bitter and throw what is right on the ground.

decisions.choice: wormwood: a bitter plant, a picture of what is bitter and harmful
decisions.reason: Wormwood is a plant with a very bitter taste (Deuteronomy 29:17; Jeremiah 9:14). Justice should be sweet and healing to those who are wronged; these judges make it bitter. 6:12 repeats the picture.

decisions.choice: bitter wormwood (B); something bitter; what is right (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced adds 'bitter' so that the point of the plant is clear. Readable says 'what is right' for tsedaqah, as the terms note settles for Amos, and 'something bitter' for wormwood, a plant few readers know (m3).

records.source: עֹשֵׂ֨ה כִימָ֜ה וּכְסִ֗יל וְהֹפֵ֤ךְ לַבֹּ֨קֶר֙ צַלְמָ֔וֶת וְי֖וֹם לַ֣יְלָה הֶחְשִׁ֑יךְ הַקּוֹרֵ֣א לְמֵֽי־הַיָּ֗ם וַֽיִּשְׁפְּכֵ֛ם עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הָאָ֖רֶץ יְהוָ֥ה שְׁמֽוֹ׃ס
records.gloss: Making Pleiades and Orion, and turning to the morning deep darkness, and day [into] night he darkens; the one calling for the waters of the sea and he pours them out on [the] face of the earth, Yahweh [is] his name.
pieces: He made the Pleiades and Orion; he turns deep darkness into morning \q and darkens day into night. \q He calls up the waters of the sea and pours them out across the face of the earth: {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} is {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} name.

L.8: [He] who made [the] Pleiades and Orion, and turns deep darkness into morning, \q and darkens day into night, \q who calls the waters of the sea and pours them out on the face of the earth, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} [is] {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} name.

R.8: {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} made the stars, the Pleiades and Orion. He turns the darkest night into morning \q and makes the day as dark as night. \q He calls for the water of the sea and pours it out on the land. {{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} is {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} name.

decisions.choice: a hymn to the LORD as Creator, set inside the accusation
decisions.reason: Verses 8-9 break into the charge of verses 7 and 10 with lines of praise in the style of a hymn, like 4:13 and 9:5-6, each ending with 'the LORD is his name'. The God whom the unjust judges ignore is the one who rules the stars, day and night, and the sea. The hymn makes the threat more fearful, not less.

decisions.choice: Pleiades and Orion: two well-known groups of stars
decisions.reason: Kimah and Kesil are named together in Job 9:9 and 38:31 too. The usual identification is the star cluster of the Pleiades and the constellation Orion. The LORD who placed them in the sky is the God Israel has to answer to.

decisions.choice: deep darkness: the darkest dark
decisions.reason: Tsalmavet means very deep darkness (Psalm 23:4; Job 10:21). It was long read as 'shadow of death', from the sound of its parts, but it is one word for thick darkness.

decisions.choice: who calls for the waters of the sea: the same line returns in 9:6
decisions.reason: The line is repeated word for word in 9:6. It may picture the rain drawn up from the sea and poured on the land, or the flood (Genesis 7). Either way the LORD rules the waters.

decisions.choice: The LORD made the stars; the darkest night (R)
decisions.reason: Readable names the LORD at the start, since the hymn otherwise begins without a subject, and says 'the stars' so that readers know what the Pleiades and Orion are (m2).

records.source: הַמַּבְלִ֥יג שֹׁ֖ד עַל־עָ֑ז וְשֹׁ֖ד עַל־מִבְצָ֥ר יָבֽוֹא׃
records.gloss: The one who makes flash devastation on [the] strong, and devastation on [the] fortress comes.
pieces: He makes destruction blaze out against the strong, \q and ruin comes upon the fortress.

L.9: who makes destruction flash out against the strong, \q so that destruction comes upon the fortress.

R.9: He suddenly destroys those who are strong, \q and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} brings ruin on their fortresses.

decisions.choice: makes flash: brings suddenly, like a flash of light
alternatives: makes destruction rise against the strong
decisions.reason: The verb is rare. In Job 9:27 and 10:20 and Psalm 39:14 it means to brighten up or to smile; here it seems to mean making destruction break out suddenly, like a flash. The sense of the line is plain even though the picture is uncertain: no strength or fortress can stand against him.

decisions.choice: suddenly destroys those who are strong (R)
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of the picture (m1) in plain words: the destruction comes suddenly.

records.source: שָׂנְא֥וּ בַשַּׁ֖עַר מוֹכִ֑יחַ וְדֹבֵ֥ר תָּמִ֖ים יְתָעֵֽבוּ׃
records.gloss: They hate in the gate one who reproves, and one who speaks with integrity they abhor.
pieces: They hate anyone who rebukes wrongdoing in court \q and detest whoever speaks honestly.

L.10: They hate the one who reproves in the gate, \q and they abhor the one who speaks with integrity.

R.10: They hate anyone who speaks up against wrong in court. \q They hate anyone who tells the truth.

decisions.choice: in the gate: in the court held at the city gate
decisions.reason: The elders of a town sat in the open space by the city gate to hear cases and give judgment (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1-11). 'In the gate' therefore means 'in court' (verses 12 and 15).

decisions.choice: the one who reproves ... the one who speaks with integrity: a witness or judge who exposes wrong and tells the truth
decisions.reason: The first word is used of someone who argues a case or rebukes a wrongdoer; the second of someone who speaks honestly, without crookedness. These are the people a fair court needs, and the powerful hate them.

decisions.choice: in court; rebukes wrongdoing (B); speaks up against wrong (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say 'in court', since many readers do not know what the city gate was used for (m1), and say what the one who 'reproves' does.

records.source: לָ֠כֵן יַ֣עַן בּוֹשַׁסְכֶ֞ם עַל־דָּ֗ל וּמַשְׂאַת־בַּר֙ תִּקְח֣וּ מִמֶּ֔נּוּ בָּתֵּ֥י גָזִ֛ית בְּנִיתֶ֖ם וְלֹא־תֵ֣שְׁבוּ בָ֑ם כַּרְמֵי־חֶ֣מֶד נְטַעְתֶּ֔ם וְלֹ֥א תִשְׁתּ֖וּ אֶת־יֵינָֽם׃
records.gloss: Therefore, because you trample on [the] poor and a levy of grain you take from him, houses of hewn stone you have built, but you will not live in them; vineyards of delight you have planted, but you will not drink their wine.
pieces: Therefore, because you trample on the poor and force them to hand over their grain, \q you have built houses of cut stone, but you will not live in them; \q you have planted fine vineyards, \q but you will not drink their wine.

L.11: Therefore, because you trample on the poor and take a levy of grain from {{gender:them|him}}, \q you have built houses of hewn stone, but you will not live in them; \q you have planted pleasant vineyards, \q but you will not drink their wine.

R.11: You crush poor people and force them to give you their grain. \q So you will never live in the fine stone houses you have built. \q You will never drink wine from the beautiful vineyards you have planted.

decisions.choice: you trample: you crush, or tax, the poor
alternatives: you levy a tax on the poor
decisions.reason: The verb occurs only here. It has usually been taken as a form of a verb meaning to trample. A word in Akkadian, the language of Assyria and Babylon, means to collect a tax, and that sense fits the parallel line, 'you take a levy of grain'. Either way the rich are living off the poor.

decisions.choice: a levy of grain: a share of the harvest taken from poor farmers
decisions.reason: Mas'at is a portion or payment that is carried off. Here the rich take part of the grain of poor farmers, perhaps as rent for land or as payment on a debt.

decisions.choice: houses you will not live in, vineyards whose wine you will not drink: the curse of the covenant
decisions.reason: Deuteronomy 28:30, 39 warns that if Israel breaks the covenant, people will build houses and not live in them, and plant vineyards and not drink their wine; Zephaniah 1:13 repeats it. Houses of hewn, squared stone were a luxury (1 Kings 7:9). In 9:14 the curse is turned round: the restored people will drink the wine of their own vineyards.

decisions.choice: them (gender setting, L); force them to hand over (B, R)
decisions.reason: 'The poor' is singular in Hebrew and stands for every poor person, so Literal uses the gender setting for 'him'. Balanced and Readable say what taking a levy meant for the poor. Readable puts the cause first and leaves out 'therefore'.

records.source: כִּ֤י יָדַ֨עְתִּי֙ רַבִּ֣ים פִּשְׁעֵיכֶ֔ם וַעֲצֻמִ֖ים חַטֹּֽאתֵיכֶ֑ם צֹרְרֵ֤י צַדִּיק֙ לֹ֣קְחֵי כֹ֔פֶר וְאֶבְיוֹנִ֖ים בַּשַּׁ֥עַר הִטּֽוּ׃
records.gloss: For I know [that] many [are] your transgressions and numerous your sins, oppressors of [the] righteous, takers of a ransom; and [the] needy in the gate they turn aside.
pieces: For I know how many your crimes are \q and how great your sins: \q you oppress the innocent and take bribes, \q and you push aside the poor in court.

L.12: For I know how many your transgressions are, \q and how numerous your sins, \q you who harass the righteous, who take a ransom, \q and turn aside the needy in the gate.

R.12: I know how many times you have sinned \q and how great your sins are. \q You treat innocent people cruelly, and you take bribes. \q You keep poor people from getting justice in court.

decisions.choice: the righteous: the one in the right, the innocent party in a case
decisions.reason: In a court, the tsaddiq is the person who is in the right. These judges harass the innocent instead of clearing them.

decisions.choice: take a ransom: take a bribe to let the guilty go
decisions.reason: Kofer is money paid to buy someone free. The law forbids taking it to spare a murderer (Numbers 35:31); here judges take it to let the guilty go or to rule against the poor (1 Samuel 12:3).

decisions.choice: turn aside the needy in the gate: deny the poor a fair hearing in court
decisions.reason: To 'turn aside' a person, or their case, is to refuse them justice (Exodus 23:6; Isaiah 10:2; see 2:7).

decisions.choice: crimes (B), sinned (R); innocent; bribes (B, R)
decisions.reason: The terms note for Amos gives pesha' as 'transgression' at Literal, 'crime' or 'rebellion' at Balanced and 'sin' at Readable. Balanced and Readable say 'innocent' for the one in the right (m1) and 'bribes' for the ransom (m2).

records.source: לָכֵ֗ן הַמַּשְׂכִּ֛יל בָּעֵ֥ת הַהִ֖יא יִדֹּ֑ם כִּ֛י עֵ֥ת רָעָ֖ה הִֽיא׃
records.gloss: Therefore the prudent at the time the that will be silent, for an evil time it [is].
pieces: So at such a time the prudent keep quiet, \q for it is an evil time.

L.13: Therefore the prudent will keep silent at that time, \q for it is an evil time.

R.13: That is why wise people keep quiet in times like these, \q because these are evil times.

decisions.choice: the prudent will keep silent: a sensible person keeps quiet, because speaking up is useless or dangerous
alternatives: the prudent will be destroyed at that time
the one who prospers will be struck dumb at that time
decisions.reason: The verse sounds like a proverb. It may describe the present: when the courts hate anyone who tells the truth (verse 10), a sensible person stays silent. Or it may look ahead to the evil time of judgment, when there will be nothing left to say. The verb can also mean to be destroyed, and the first word can mean one who prospers. Amos himself does not keep silent, so the line may be a bitter remark rather than advice.

decisions.choice: an evil time: a time of wickedness, and of the disaster it brings
decisions.reason: Ra'ah can mean moral evil or calamity, and both fit: the time is wicked, and disaster is coming because of it. Micah 2:3 uses the same phrase of a time of disaster.

records.source: דִּרְשׁוּ־ט֥וֹב וְאַל־רָ֖ע לְמַ֣עַן תִּֽחְי֑וּ וִיהִי־כֵ֞ן יְהוָ֧ה אֱלֹהֵֽי־צְבָא֛וֹת אִתְּכֶ֖ם כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר אֲמַרְתֶּֽם׃
records.gloss: Seek good and not evil, so that you may live, and so Yahweh God of hosts will be with you, just as you have said.
pieces: Seek good and not evil, so that you may live, \q and so that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} God of Armies may truly be with you, as you claim {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is.

L.14: Seek good and not evil, so that you may live; \q and so {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} God of hosts will be with you, just as you have said.

R.14: Seek what is good, not what is evil, so that you will live. \q Then {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} God of Armies will really be with you, as you say {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is.

decisions.choice: seek good: doing good is the way of seeking the LORD
decisions.reason: Verses 4 and 6 say 'Seek me' and 'Seek the LORD'; here it is 'Seek good'. Seeking God and doing what is right are one thing, not two.

decisions.choice: just as you have said: the people claim that God is with them
decisions.reason: The people said that the LORD God of hosts was with them, perhaps in their worship or their battle cries, and felt secure (compare Micah 3:11). Amos turns the slogan into a condition: he will be with them if they seek good.

decisions.choice: the LORD God of hosts (L); the LORD God of Armies (B, R)
decisions.reason: YHWH 'elohe tseva'ot is the title 'the LORD of hosts' with 'God' added. It keeps the wording settled for 'the God of hosts' (Hosea 12:6): 'hosts' at Literal, 'Armies' at Balanced and Readable. The hosts are the armies of heaven and earth that the LORD commands.

decisions.choice: as you claim he is (B); as you say he is (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the people 'have said', that the LORD is with them (m2).

records.source: שִׂנְאוּ־רָע֙ וְאֶ֣הֱבוּ ט֔וֹב וְהַצִּ֥יגוּ בַשַּׁ֖עַר מִשְׁפָּ֑ט אוּלַ֗י יֶֽחֱנַ֛ן יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵֽי־צְבָא֖וֹת שְׁאֵרִ֥ית יוֹסֵֽף׃ס
records.gloss: Hate evil and love good, and set up in the gate justice; perhaps Yahweh God of hosts will be gracious [to the] remnant of Joseph.
pieces: Hate evil and love good; \q establish justice in the courts. \q It may be that {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} God of Armies will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.

L.15: Hate evil and love good, \q and establish justice in the gate; \q perhaps {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} God of hosts will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.

R.15: Hate what is evil and love what is good. \q Make sure that the courts are fair. \q Then perhaps {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} God of Armies will be kind to the people of Israel who are left.

decisions.choice: perhaps: there is hope, but no promise
decisions.reason: Even if the people turn, the LORD is not bound to spare them; his mercy cannot be taken for granted (Joel 2:14; Jonah 3:9; Zephaniah 2:3). The offer is real, but it is not a bargain.

decisions.choice: the remnant of Joseph: those who will be left after the judgment
decisions.reason: Amos has already said that only a tenth will survive (verse 3). The remnant is what remains of the northern kingdom, Joseph's house (verse 6). Even the hope he holds out is for survivors.

decisions.choice: in the courts (B); make sure that the courts are fair; the people of Israel who are left (R)
decisions.reason: 'In the gate' means in court (verse 10). Readable says 'the people of Israel who are left' for 'the remnant of Joseph' (5:6).

records.source: לָ֠כֵן כֹּֽה־אָמַ֨ר יְהוָ֜ה אֱלֹהֵ֤י צְבָאוֹת֙ אֲדֹנָ֔י בְּכָל־רְחֹב֣וֹת מִסְפֵּ֔ד וּבְכָל־חוּצ֖וֹת יֹאמְר֣וּ הוֹ־ה֑וֹ וְקָרְא֤וּ אִכָּר֙ אֶל־אֵ֔בֶל וּמִסְפֵּ֖ד אֶל־י֥וֹדְעֵי נֶֽהִי׃
records.gloss: Therefore thus says Yahweh God of hosts, [the] Lord: in all squares [there will be] wailing, and in all streets they will say, Alas! Alas! And they will call [the] farmer to mourning, and wailing to those who know lamentation.
pieces: Therefore {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} God of Armies, the Lord, says this: \q There will be wailing in every square, \q and in every street people will cry, "Alas! Alas!" \q They will call the farmers to mourn \q and the professional mourners to wail.

L.16: Therefore thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} God of hosts, the Lord: \q In all the squares [there will be] wailing, \q and in all the streets they will say, "Alas! Alas!" \q They will call the farmer to mourning, \q and [call] to wailing those skilled in lament.

R.16: So this is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} God of Armies, the Lord, says: \q People will be crying in all the town squares. \q In every street they will cry out, "How sad! How sad!" \q They will call farmers in from the fields to weep. \q They will call for those who are paid to mourn for the dead.

decisions.choice: those who know lamentation: professional mourners
decisions.reason: At a funeral, women skilled in lament were called in to lead the weeping (Jeremiah 9:16-17; 2 Chronicles 35:25). There will be so many dead that even farmers are called from the fields to mourn, and the professional mourners will be needed everywhere.

decisions.choice: Alas! Alas!: the cry of mourning for the dead
decisions.reason: Ho is the cry of grief at a funeral (1 Kings 13:30; Jeremiah 22:18), related to hoy, 'woe' (5:18).

decisions.choice: the Lord: a further title after 'the LORD God of hosts'
decisions.reason: The title is unusual: Adonai, 'the Lord', stands at the end, after 'the LORD God of hosts'. It stresses that the one who speaks is master over all.

decisions.choice: How sad! How sad! (R); in from the fields (R)
decisions.reason: The funeral cry is 'Alas' at Literal and Balanced and 'How sad' at Readable, as Jeremiah 22:18. Readable adds 'in from the fields' to show why farmers are named.

records.heading: Wailing in every street

records.source: וּבְכָל־כְּרָמִ֖ים מִסְפֵּ֑ד כִּֽי־אֶעֱבֹ֥ר בְּקִרְבְּךָ֖ אָמַ֥ר יְהוָֽה׃ס
records.gloss: And in all vineyards [there will be] wailing, for I will pass through your midst, says Yahweh.
pieces: There will be wailing in every vineyard, \q for I will pass through the middle of you, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

L.17: And in all the vineyards [there will be] wailing, \q for I will pass through your midst, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

R.17: People will cry in all the vineyards, \q because I will come through your land to punish you, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.

decisions.choice: I will pass through your midst: as the LORD passed through Egypt on the night of the Passover
decisions.reason: In Exodus 12:12 the LORD says 'I will pass through the land of Egypt' to strike the firstborn. Now he will pass through Israel in judgment, as if Israel had become Egypt. Compare 7:8 and 8:2, where he says he will no longer 'pass by' them, that is, spare them.

decisions.choice: wailing in the vineyards: even the places of joy will be places of mourning
decisions.reason: The grape harvest was a time of singing and shouting (Isaiah 16:10; Judges 9:27). Now there will be wailing there too.

decisions.choice: come through your land to punish you (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says why the LORD will pass through (m1).

records.source: ה֥וֹי הַמִּתְאַוִּ֖ים אֶת־י֣וֹם יְהוָ֑ה לָמָּה־זֶּ֥ה לָכֶ֛ם י֥וֹם יְהוָ֖ה הוּא־חֹ֥שֶׁךְ וְלֹא־אֽוֹר׃
records.gloss: Woe [to] those who desire the day of Yahweh! Why [is] this to you, the day of Yahweh? It [is] darkness and not light.
pieces: Woe to you who long for the day of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}! \q Why do you want the day of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}? It will be darkness, not light.

L.18: Woe, you who long for the day of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}! \q What [good is] the day of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} to you? It [is] darkness, and not light.

R.18: How terrible it will be for you who want the day of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} to come! \q Why do you want that day? It will be a day of darkness, not light.

decisions.choice: the day of the LORD: the day when the LORD acts in power, which Israel expected to bring victory and Amos says will bring judgment on Israel
decisions.reason: This is the earliest use of 'the day of the LORD' among the prophets; the main note is at Joel 1:15. Amos's hearers knew the phrase and looked forward to that day as the time when the LORD would rise up to defeat their enemies and bless his people. Amos turns their hope upside down: the day will be darkness for Israel itself, because Israel too is among the guilty. Later prophets take up the same warning (Isaiah 13:6, 9; Zephaniah 1:14-18; Joel 2:1-2).

decisions.choice: woe: the cry of mourning over people as good as dead
decisions.reason: Hoy is the cry raised at a funeral (compare 5:16). Spoken over the living, it announces their death. Isaiah's 'woe' sayings use it the same way (Isaiah 5:8).

decisions.choice: darkness, not light: disaster, not deliverance
decisions.reason: Light stands for safety, blessing and salvation, darkness for disaster and judgment (Isaiah 9:1; 13:10).

decisions.choice: Woe, you who (L); Woe to you who (B); How terrible it will be for you who (R); the day of the LORD at every level
decisions.reason: Hoy follows Isaiah's wording at each level, and 'the day of the LORD' keeps the same words at every level, as Isaiah 13:6. The Hebrew says 'those who long for' and then turns to 'you'; the English uses 'you' throughout.

records.heading: The day of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}

records.source: כַּאֲשֶׁ֨ר יָנ֥וּס אִישׁ֙ מִפְּנֵ֣י הָאֲרִ֔י וּפְגָע֖וֹ הַדֹּ֑ב וּבָ֣א הַבַּ֔יִת וְסָמַ֤ךְ יָדוֹ֙ עַל־הַקִּ֔יר וּנְשָׁכ֖וֹ הַנָּחָֽשׁ׃
records.gloss: As when a man flees from before the lion, and the bear meets him; and he goes [into] the house and leans his hand on the wall, and the snake bites him.
pieces: It will be as when a man runs from a lion \q and a bear meets him, \q or he goes home \q and leans his hand against the wall, \q and a snake bites him.

L.19: As if a man fled from the lion, \q and the bear met him; \q and he went into the house \q and leaned his hand against the wall, \q and the snake bit him.

R.19: It will be like a man who runs away from a lion, \q only to meet a bear. \q Or he gets home safely \q and leans his hand against the wall, \q and a snake bites him.

decisions.choice: a picture of the day of the LORD: no way of escape
decisions.reason: The man escapes one danger only to meet another, and when he reaches the safety of his own house, he is bitten there. So it will be on the day of the LORD: Israel will not escape, wherever it turns. Amos has used the picture of the lion before (3:4, 8, 12), and 9:1-4 says the same without a picture.

decisions.choice: only to; gets home safely (R)
decisions.reason: Readable adds 'only to' and 'safely' to bring out the point of the picture: each time the man thinks he has escaped (m1).

records.source: הֲלֹא־חֹ֛שֶׁךְ י֥וֹם יְהוָ֖ה וְלֹא־א֑וֹר וְאָפֵ֖ל וְלֹא־נֹ֥גַֽהּ לֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: [Is] not darkness the day of Yahweh, and not light, and gloom and no brightness to it?
pieces: Will not the day of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} be darkness, not light, \q pitch dark, with no brightness in it?

L.20: Is not the day of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} darkness, and not light, \q and gloom with no brightness in it?

R.20: Yes, the day of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will be darkness, not light. \q It will be completely dark, with no light at all.

decisions.choice: Is not ...?: a question that expects the answer 'Yes, it is'
decisions.reason: The question repeats the end of verse 18 and drives it home. The answer is not in doubt.

decisions.choice: gloom ... no brightness: thick darkness without a glimmer
decisions.reason: 'Afel is the deep dark of night (Isaiah 59:9). Nogah is brightness or the first glow of light; not even that will be left.

decisions.choice: a statement, not a question (R)
decisions.reason: Readable gives the answer the question expects (m1) as a plain statement.

records.source: שָׂנֵ֥אתִי מָאַ֖סְתִּי חַגֵּיכֶ֑ם וְלֹ֥א אָרִ֖יחַ בְּעַצְּרֹֽתֵיכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: I hate, I reject your feasts, and I do not delight in your assemblies.
pieces: I hate, I despise your festivals; \q I take no pleasure in your sacred assemblies.

L.21: I hate, I reject your feasts, \q and I take no delight in your solemn assemblies.

R.21: I hate your religious festivals. I cannot stand them. \q I am not pleased with your special meetings for worship.

decisions.choice: the LORD rejects worship offered by those who do injustice
decisions.reason: Amos is not rejecting worship as such; verses 21-24 set worship against justice. The same is said in Isaiah 1:11-17, Hosea 6:6 and Micah 6:6-8: sacrifices offered by people who oppress the poor are hateful to God.

decisions.choice: feasts and assemblies: the pilgrimage festivals and the gatherings for worship
decisions.reason: Chag is a pilgrimage feast, such as Passover, Weeks and Booths, when the people went to the shrines (Exodus 23:14-17). 'Atsarah is a holy gathering on a feast day (Leviticus 23:36; Isaiah 1:13).

decisions.choice: I take no delight: literally 'I will not smell'
decisions.reason: The verb means to smell, and is used of the LORD accepting the smell of an offering (Genesis 8:21). Leviticus 26:31 warns, 'I will not smell your pleasing aromas.' He refuses the scent of their sacrifices.

decisions.choice: religious festivals; special meetings for worship (R)
decisions.reason: Readable says what kind of feasts and assemblies are meant (m2).

records.source: כִּ֣י אִם־תַּעֲלוּ־לִ֥י עֹל֛וֹת וּמִנְחֹתֵיכֶ֖ם לֹ֣א אֶרְצֶ֑ה וְשֶׁ֥לֶם מְרִיאֵיכֶ֖ם לֹ֥א אַבִּֽיט׃
records.gloss: For if you offer up to me burnt offerings and your grain offerings, I will not accept [them]; and the peace offering of your fatlings I will not look at.
pieces: Even if you sacrifice burnt offerings and grain offerings to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, I will not accept them; \q I will not look at the peace offerings of your fattened animals.

L.22: Even if you offer up to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} burnt offerings and your grain offerings, I will not accept [them]; \q and the peace offerings of your fattened animals I will not look at.

R.22: Even if you bring {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} burnt offerings and grain offerings, I will not accept them. \q I will not even look at the fat animals you bring as peace offerings.

decisions.choice: burnt offerings, grain offerings, peace offerings: the main kinds of sacrifice
decisions.reason: A burnt offering was burned whole on the altar (Leviticus 1). A grain offering was flour or grain with oil (Leviticus 2). The peace offering was shared: part was burned, and the worshipers ate the rest in a meal (Leviticus 3; 7:11-15). The LORD rejects all three.

decisions.choice: accept ... look at: receive with favor
decisions.reason: Ratsah is the word for the LORD accepting an offering and the one who brings it (Leviticus 1:4). To 'look at' an offering is to regard it with favor, as the LORD looked at Abel's offering (Genesis 4:4). He will do neither.

records.source: הָסֵ֥ר מֵעָלַ֖י הֲמ֣וֹן שִׁרֶ֑יךָ וְזִמְרַ֥ת נְבָלֶ֖יךָ לֹ֥א אֶשְׁמָֽע׃
records.gloss: Remove from me the noise of your songs, and the music of your harps I will not listen to.
pieces: Take the noise of your songs away from {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}; \q I will not listen to the music of your harps.

L.23: Take away from {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} the noise of your songs; \q the music of your harps I will not listen to.

R.23: Take your noisy songs away from {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}! \q I will not listen to the music of your harps.

decisions.choice: noise: the loud din of a crowd
decisions.reason: Hamon is the roar of a crowd or of many voices. The temple songs that the singers think beautiful are only noise to the LORD.

decisions.choice: remove ... your songs ... your harps: spoken to the people as one
decisions.reason: The command and the word 'your' in this verse are singular, though verses 21-22 address the people as 'you' plural. The LORD speaks to Israel as one worshiper, or to each one in it.

records.source: וְיִגַּ֥ל כַּמַּ֖יִם מִשְׁפָּ֑ט וּצְדָקָ֖ה כְּנַ֥חַל אֵיתָֽן׃
records.gloss: But let roll like the waters justice, and righteousness like a stream ever-flowing.
pieces: Instead, let justice roll on like water, \q and righteousness like a stream that never runs dry.

L.24: But let justice roll on like the waters, \q and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.

R.24: Instead, let justice flow like a river. \q Let what is right keep flowing like a stream that never dries up.

decisions.choice: justice and righteousness: as in 5:7, fair judgment and right dealing
decisions.reason: This is what the LORD wants in place of the feasts of verses 21-23: justice and right dealing running through the life of the people as freely and constantly as water. In 5:7 the same pair was turned into bitter wormwood.

decisions.choice: an ever-flowing stream: a stream that does not dry up in summer
decisions.reason: Most streams in the land ran only in the rainy season and were dry beds in summer. 'Etan means constant or lasting. Justice is to be like the rare stream that never fails, not like the ones that run for a while and then vanish (compare Jeremiah 15:18).

decisions.choice: let it roll: a command or wish, not a threat
alternatives: a threat: judgment will roll over them like a flood
decisions.reason: The verb form expresses a wish or command, 'let it roll'. The verse is usually read as what the LORD wants instead of empty worship. Some read it as a threat, that judgment (mishpat) will sweep over the people like a flood; but in 5:7 and 6:12 the pair 'justice and righteousness' is what the people should do, which favors the usual reading.

decisions.choice: a stream that never runs dry (B); flow like a river; what is right (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what 'ever-flowing' means (m2). Readable says 'what is right' for tsedaqah, as the terms note settles for Amos, and 'flow like a river' for 'roll on like waters'.

records.source: הַזְּבָחִ֨ים וּמִנְחָ֜ה הִֽגַּשְׁתֶּם־לִ֧י בַמִּדְבָּ֛ר אַרְבָּעִ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה בֵּ֥ית יִשְׂרָאֵֽל׃
records.gloss: [Was it] sacrifices and offering [that] you brought near to me in the wilderness forty years, house of Israel?
pieces: Was it sacrifices and offerings that you brought {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} during the forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel?

L.25: Did you bring sacrifices and offerings to {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} in the wilderness forty years, house of Israel?

R.25: People of Israel, during the forty years in the desert, was it sacrifices and offerings that you brought {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}?

decisions.choice: did you bring me sacrifices ...?: a question expecting the answer 'no', or 'not only sacrifices'
alternatives: you did bring sacrifices, but you also carried other gods (read with verse 26)
decisions.reason: The question puts 'sacrifices and offerings' first for emphasis, and it expects a negative answer, but it is not clear how far that answer goes. It may mean that in the forty years in the wilderness Israel did not offer sacrifices at all, so the bond between the LORD and his people never depended on them. Or it may mean that what the LORD wanted then was not sacrifice alone but obedience (Jeremiah 7:22-23). Either way, it supports verses 21-24: sacrifices cannot take the place of justice.

decisions.choice: quoted by Stephen in Acts 7:42-43
decisions.reason: Stephen quotes verses 25-27 in his speech (Acts 7:42-43), following the Greek translation. There the question is clearly 'You did not offer me ... did you?', and it is part of his account of Israel's turning to idols in the wilderness. The wording here is translated from the Hebrew; the differences in verses 26-27 are noted there.

decisions.choice: Was it sacrifices and offerings that ...? (B, R); desert (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable keep the Hebrew's emphasis on 'sacrifices and offerings' by putting them first in a 'Was it ...?' question. Readable says 'desert' for 'wilderness'.

records.source: וּנְשָׂאתֶ֗ם אֵ֚ת סִכּ֣וּת מַלְכְּכֶ֔ם וְאֵ֖ת כִּיּ֣וּן צַלְמֵיכֶ֑ם כּוֹכַב֙ אֱלֹ֣הֵיכֶ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר עֲשִׂיתֶ֖ם לָכֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And you will lift up Sikkuth your king and Kiyyun your images, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves.
pieces: So you will carry off Sikkuth, your king, \q and Kiyyun, your idols, \q the star of your god, \q which you made for yourselves.

L.26: And you will lift up Sikkuth your king \q and Kiyyun your images, \q the star of your god, \q that you made for yourselves.

R.26: You will have to carry away your idols, \q Sikkuth, the god you call your king, \q and Kiyyun, your star god. \q You made them yourselves.

decisions.choice: you will lift up: you will carry your idols with you into exile
alternatives: you lifted up (past): you carried these gods in procession, continuing the question of verse 25
decisions.reason: The verb form most often looks ahead, and verse 27 goes on 'and I will send you into exile'. Read so, the people will have to carry their own idols on the road into exile, gods that cannot carry them (compare Isaiah 46:1-2). The same form can also describe the past, and then the verse says that Israel carried other gods in procession, then or in the wilderness. The Greek translation, quoted in Acts 7:43, takes it as past.

decisions.choice: Sikkuth and Kiyyun: Sakkuth and Kaiwan, gods of Mesopotamia linked with the planet Saturn
alternatives: the booth (sukkat) of your king and the stand (kiyyun) of your images
decisions.reason: Sakkuth and Kaiwan are known as names of Mesopotamian star gods, and Kaiwan was a name of the planet Saturn. The Hebrew vowels make both names sound like shiqquts, 'detestable thing', probably as a mark of contempt. With other vowels, the words can mean 'the booth of your king' and 'the stand of your images'. The Greek translation read the first as 'the tent of Moloch' and the second as the name of a god, 'Rephan' (Acts 7:43).

decisions.choice: the star of your god: gods worshiped as stars
decisions.reason: The line describes the gods of the first half as star gods. Worship of the 'host of heaven' is forbidden in Deuteronomy 4:19, and 2 Kings 17:16 names it among the sins for which the northern kingdom fell. Stephen speaks of it in Acts 7:42.

decisions.choice: idols (B); the god you call your king; your star god (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced says 'idols' for tselem, 'images', since these are images of gods. Readable says what each name stands for (m2, m3) and that the people will 'have to' carry them (m1).

records.gloss: And I will send you into exile beyond Damascus, says Yahweh, God of hosts [is] his name.
pieces: So I will take you into exile beyond Damascus, \q says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; the God of Armies is {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} name.

L.27: And I will drive you into exile beyond Damascus, \q says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; the God of hosts [is] {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} name.

R.27: I will send you away as captives to a land far beyond Damascus. \q That is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says. His name is the God of Armies.

decisions.choice: beyond Damascus: to Assyria
decisions.reason: Damascus, the capital of Aram, lay north-east of Israel. Beyond it lay Assyria, which took the people of the northern kingdom into exile in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:6). Amos never names Assyria, but the direction is plain.

decisions.choice: Stephen's quotation reads 'beyond Babylon'
decisions.reason: In Acts 7:43 Stephen says 'beyond Babylon' in place of 'beyond Damascus'. The Greek translation of Amos has 'Damascus', so the change is Stephen's own: he applies the warning to the later exile of Judah to Babylon, which his hearers knew.

decisions.choice: the God of hosts is his name (L); the God of Armies (B, R)
decisions.reason: 'The God of hosts' is 'the God of Armies' at Balanced and Readable, as settled for the Twelve. Readable makes the closing words a sentence of their own.
